docs.title: Your first run
docs.text: This page walks through the first ten minutes of the game and explains what each system is showing you.

docs.title: The title screen
docs.text:
The title screen offers New game, Continue, Load game, Preferences and Quit. If no save exists, Continue and Load game are disabled.

Starting a new game creates a fresh HarvestSaveData and drops you into the Harvesthold.

docs.title: The Harvesthold
docs.text:
The hub is a 40 × 30 unit walled settlement with:

Object Location Purpose Harvest Altar Centre-north Ceremonies, the quest chain's first objective Portal East side Begins an expedition into the Fallow Oracle Near the altar Story dialogue and guidance Merchant East of the altar Buys and sells gear Companions Roaming Work, eat, sleep, heal, socialise

The HUD along the top shows the day, wood, stone, pearls, food, grace, companions, omens, meals, herbs, medicine, potions, bombs and the current rite.

docs.title: 1. Hold a hymn
docs.text:
Walk to the Harvest Altar and press E. Choose Hymn.

A hymn costs grace and food, grants devotion and progresses the quest chain. It also raises the mood of nearby companions. The first quest stage after the farm is "Hold a hymn at the Harvest Altar".

docs.title: 2. Build a farm
docs.text:
Press B to open the build menu. Choose Rose Garden (the farm).

  • Move the cursor to position the ghost.
  • Q rotates.
  • E or left click confirms; Esc cancels.

The farm costs wood (and needs a worker to produce at full rate). It generates food on a 12-second interval.

docs.title: 3. Meet your companions
docs.text:
Press F for the roster. Each companion has:

  • a name and trait (Loyal, Hardworking, Glutton, Devout, Sickly, Lazy);
  • hunger, loyalty and exhaustion;
  • a job, a bed and a priority;
  • relationships (friend, partner, parents, children).

Select a companion to feed them, assign a job, assign a bed, or send them to the Reflection Chamber. Companions who are starving, exhausted or sick work slower and lose loyalty.

docs.title: 4. Enter the Fallow
docs.text:
Press C to open the Pilgrimage Map. Act I is available; Acts II and III are locked until the previous Warden falls.

Choose Begin pilgrimage. You appear in the first room of a generated floor.

  • Clear the room's husks to unlock the doors.
  • Collect keys; some doors are locked.
  • Shrines, shops, treasure, puzzles and curses appear as you explore.
  • Find the stairs to descend.

docs.title: 5. Fight
docs.text:
Input Action Space Attack with the current armament Left Shift Dodge (brief invulnerability) X Cast the current rite G Throw a bomb Q / Z Cycle armament / rite H Drink a potion

Armaments have distinct rhythms: the Fan Blade is a fast four-hit combo, the Bell Hammer is a single wide swing that hits everything, the Thorn Claws heal on hit. Rites are area effects with cooldowns.

docs.title: 6. Break a Warden
docs.text:
Each act ends with a Warden. The three are:

Act Realm Warden I Ashen Orchard The Gilded Stag II Drowned Conservatory The Mire Queen III Ember Citadel The Obsidian Sultan

Wardens have multiple phases and telegraphed attacks. Their arenas change with the act. Defeating one unlocks the next act and grants devotion.

docs.title: 7. Save and return
docs.text:
• F5 saves to the active slot; F9 loads.
  • Autosave is on by default (Preferences → Autosave).
  • Returning through the portal ends the expedition; loot is kept.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Build a Kitchen Pavilion to make feasts cheaper.
  • Build a Reflection Chamber to resolve a companion's crisis.
  • Collect omens after boss fights; they change the run's rules.
  • Spend devotion on meta-upgrades from the pilgrimage map.
  • Press K in the hub for the catalog codex of everything you have seen.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page takes you from the store download to a running project. It assumes nothing is installed yet.

docs.title: 1. Install Unity
docs.text:
You need Unity 6000.6.6f1 or a newer Unity 6 release.

  1. Install Unity Hub from https://unity.com/download.
  2. In Hub, open Installs → Install Editor → Archive.
  3. Pick 6000.6.6f1 and install it with:
    • Windows Build Support (Mono) or macOS Build Support (Mono)
    • Linux Build Support (Mono) if you target Linux

Module choice

The template builds with the Mono scripting backend, so you do not need the IL2CPP toolchains to run or build it. Add IL2CPP later if you want it for release builds.

docs.title: 2. Get the project
docs.text:
Download the package from the Unity Asset Store (My Assets → Download), or unzip the project archive you received.

You should end up with a folder containing:

Assets/
Packages/
ProjectSettings/
README.md
CHANGELOG.md
Tools/

If you received a .unitypackage instead, create a new 3D (URP) project in Unity Hub first, then import the package into it.

docs.title: 3. Add it to Unity Hub
docs.text:
1. Open Unity Hub → Projects.
  2. Click Add → Add project from disk.
  3. Select the folder that contains Assets, Packages and ProjectSettings.
  4. Open it with 6000.6.6f1.

Do not create a new project inside the template

docs.title: 4. First import
docs.text:
Unity resolves the package manifest and compiles the scripts. Expect:

  • a progress bar for the first import (one to three minutes on a laptop);
  • no external downloads beyond the declared Unity packages;
  • an empty Console when it finishes.

If the Console shows error CS…, the project is being opened with an unsupported Unity version. Check ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt.

docs.title: 5. Open the scene and play
docs.text:
1. In the Project window, open Assets/ChosenOfTheHarvest/Scenes/ChosenOfTheHarvest.unity.
  2. Press Play.
  3. Choose New game.

The scene contains a single Game object. Everything else — camera, hub, HUD, companions, audio — is created at runtime by HarvestGame.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: SoundDirector is a single MonoBehaviour with two AudioSources and no middleware: one looping source for music, one PlayOneShot source for effects. It synthesises a full placeholder palette in code at startup, then replaces each clip with the same-named file from Resources/Audio when one exists. That means the game is audible with zero audio assets, and shipping final audio is a file swap rather than a code change.

docs.title: The 21 keys
docs.text:
SoundBank.UsedKeys is the authoritative list. It holds five music keys and sixteen effect keys, in the order below.

Key Category Shipped .wav Generated fallback Used for music_hub music 8 s 24 s the Harvesthold, from Awake music_dungeon music 8 s 24 s expedition rooms that are not Warden rooms music_boss0 music 8 s 16 s Ashen Orchard Warden music_boss1 music 8 s 16 s Drowned Conservatory Warden music_boss2 music 8 s 16 s Ember Citadel Warden swing SFX 0.18 s 0.22 s every player attack hit SFX 0.16 s 0.20 s a husk or projectile impact hurt SFX 0.40 s 0.42 s the Sovereign takes damage die SFX 0.80 s 0.95 s a husk or a Warden falls gather SFX 0.30 s 0.28 s a resource node is struck build SFX 0.50 s 0.62 s a sanctum is placed pickup SFX 0.25 s 0.36 s loot, pearls, equipment chest SFX 1.60 s 0.95 s a chest opens ceremony SFX 2.40 s 2.80 s ceremonies, oaths, Warden defeats feast SFX 1.40 s 2.40 s Feast and Ceremony of Plenty sacrifice SFX 1.20 s 1.90 s a sacrifice is accepted portal SFX 0.80 s 1.25 s entering or leaving an expedition sharpen SFX 0.35 s 0.55 s Sharpen blade at the altar ui SFX 0.08 s 0.09 s menu ticks and confirmations error SFX 0.20 s 0.28 s a refused action slam SFX 0.45 s 0.65 s Bell Golem and Warden ground slams

The "generated fallback" column is the duration passed to Make(...); the shipped durations are what the mono 22,050 Hz files in Resources/Audio measure. The shipped file always wins, so those are the lengths you hear in a clean checkout.

The palette is prose, not data

SoundBank.Palette is a parallel array of one-line descriptions ("warm harp and low strings", "mire queen reeds"). SourceOf(key) returns the description at the same index, and nothing in the game branches on it. It exists so the audio intent survives in source control while the clips are placeholders.

docs.title: Where clips come from
docs.text:
Two passes fill the same dictionary in Awake:

void Awake()
{
    Instance = this;

    musicSource = gameObject.AddComponent<AudioSource>();
    musicSource.playOnAwake = false;
    musicSource.loop = true;
    musicSource.spatialBlend = 0f;
    musicSource.volume = 0.34f;

    sfxSource = gameObject.AddComponent<AudioSource>();
    sfxSource.playOnAwake = false;
    sfxSource.spatialBlend = 0f;
    sfxSource.volume = 0.75f;

    BuildClips();

    Muted = PlayerPrefs.GetInt(MutePref, 0) == 1;
    ApplyMute();
    ApplyVolumes();
}

BuildClips() synthesises all 21 clips with AudioClip.Create(...) at a fixed Rate = 22050, mono, using sine/square/saw/noise generators. Noise(int) is a deterministic hash, so every launch sounds identical. Music gets a 0.12 s fade on both edges (FadeEdges) so an 8-second loop does not click.

Then LoadPlaceholderClips() overwrites them from Resources:

foreach (var key in keys)
{
    var clip = Resources.Load<AudioClip>("Audio/" + key);
    if (clip == null)
    {
        MissingPlaceholderCount++;
        continue;
    }
    clips[key] = clip;
    PlaceholderClipCount++;
}

The naming convention is therefore exact and extension-free: a file at Assets/ChosenOfTheHarvest/Resources/Audio/music_hub.wav loads as Resources.Load<AudioClip>("Audio/music_hub"). A renamed file simply does not load, and the generated clip keeps playing.

Four counters expose the result, which the smoke test logs:

Property Meaning ClipCount keys currently in the dictionary — 21 in a clean project UsedClipCount SoundBank.UsedKeys.Length — always 21 PlaceholderClipCount keys whose clip came from Resources/Audio MissingPlaceholderCount keys that fell back to the synth

docs.title: Music vs SFX
docs.text:
The two sources have different jobs, and only the music source is asked to loop.

Source Loop Volume base API Clips musicSource yes 0.34 PlayMusic(key) the five music_* keys sfxSource no 0.75 Play(key, volume, pitch) / Sfx(...) the sixteen effect keys

PlayMusic is idempotent: it returns early when the requested key is already playing, so calling it every room does not restart the track.

public void PlayMusic(string key)
{
    if (musicSource == null) return;
    if (!clips.TryGetValue(key, out var clip) || clip == null) return;
    if (currentMusic == key && musicSource.isPlaying) return;

    currentMusic = key;
    musicSource.clip = clip;
    musicSource.loop = true;
    musicSource.Play();
}

The call sites are few enough to list in full:

Moment Key Where Boot, before the title screen music_hub HarvestGame.Awake() Enter an expedition music_dungeon HarvestGame.EnterExpedition(int) Every room transition music_boss<act> in a Warden room, else music_dungeon Expedition.EnterRoom (in Dungeon.cs) Warden dies music_dungeon Expedition boss-death routine Return to the hub music_hub HarvestGame.ExitExpedition(bool)

music_boss0/1/2 are selected by act index with string concatenation — "music_boss" + ActIndex — so a fourth act needs a fourth key and clip.

docs.title: Effects and the call pattern
docs.text:
Effects go through a static helper, which keeps combat code free of null checks:

public static void Sfx(string name, float volume = 1f, float pitch = 1f)
{
    if (Instance != null) Instance.Play(name, volume, pitch);
}

public void Play(string name, float volume = 1f, float pitch = 1f)
{
    if (Muted || sfxSource == null) return;
    if (!clips.TryGetValue(name, out var clip) || clip == null) return;

    sfxSource.pitch = Mathf.Clamp(pitch, 0.55f, 1.9f);
    sfxSource.PlayOneShot(clip, Mathf.Clamp01(volume));
}

Three behaviours follow from that:

  • Pitch is a shared property, not per-shot. PlayOneShot inherits the source pitch, so two overlapping effects use the pitch of the most recent call. Variation is still useful for single hits.
  • Unknown keys fail silently. No log, no exception — a typo is a missing sound, not a crash.
  • Volume is clamped to 0-1 and multiplied by the source volume routing below, so passing 1f does not mean "full scale".

Typical arguments in the source: ui at 0.55f, a combo swing at 0.7f with pitch 0.85f + comboIndex * 0.04f, die at 1f and pitch 0.62f for a Warden, error at 0.6f.

docs.title: Volume routing
docs.text:
Volumes are multiplied in two stages: a per-source base, then the player's master and channel values.

void ApplyVolumes()
{
    if (musicSource != null) musicSource.volume = 0.34f * masterVolume * musicVolume;
    if (sfxSource != null) sfxSource.volume = 0.75f * masterVolume * sfxVolume;
}
Value Default Source masterVolume 0.85 Preferences.MasterVolume, key choth_settings_master musicVolume 0.65 Preferences.MusicVolume, key choth_settings_music sfxVolume 0.85 Preferences.SfxVolume, key choth_settings_sfx music base 0.34 Awake SFX base 0.75 Awake

With default settings that is an effective music level of 0.34 × 0.85 × 0.65 ≈ 0.188 and SFX of 0.75 × 0.85 × 0.85 ≈ 0.542. The SFX source is intentionally the louder of the two.

Preferences.Apply() pushes the three values on boot and after every change:

SoundDirector.Instance?.SetVolumes(MasterVolume, MusicVolume, SfxVolume);

The settings menu does not use a slider. HarvestGame.ShowPreferences() cycles each volume in ten-point steps through CycleVolume, which rounds to a tenth, adds one, wraps at 11 and divides back:

static float CycleVolume(float value)
{
    int step = Mathf.RoundToInt(value * 10f);
    step = (step + 1) % 11;
    return step / 10f;
}

Pressing the row eleven times returns to where it started, and 0% is reachable.

docs.title: Mute
docs.text:
M is a binding, not a hard-coded key: Bindings.Action.Mute defaults to Key.M and can be reassigned. HarvestGame.Update calls ToggleMute(), which delegates to the director and toasts the new state:

public void ToggleMute()
{
    bool muted = Audio.ToggleMute();
    HarvestHudRef.Toast(muted ? "Audio muted   •   press M" : "Audio on   •   press M");
}

Mute is stored separately from the settings block, in choth_audio_muted, and survives restarts:

const string MutePref = "choth_audio_muted";

public bool ToggleMute()
{
    Muted = !Muted;
    PlayerPrefs.SetInt(MutePref, Muted ? 1 : 0);
    PlayerPrefs.Save();
    ApplyMute();
    return Muted;
}

ApplyMute() sets mute on both sources rather than zeroing their volumes, so un-muting restores the exact levels the player had set. Play also returns early while muted, which keeps PlayOneShot calls from stacking up silently.

Mute is not a volume row

Mute is not part of Preferences and does not appear in the settings menu. Only M (or SoundDirector.SetMuted) changes it. If you add a "Mute" row to the menu, drive it through SetMuted, not Preferences, or the two states will disagree after a restart.

docs.title: Adding or replacing a clip
docs.text:
Replacing is a file swap. Keep the base name identical to the key, drop the file into Assets/ChosenOfTheHarvest/Resources/Audio/, and let Unity import it as an AudioClip. No code changes, no array edits, and the old synth version stops being used automatically. Music files should be loop-safe; the source has loop = true, and the code does not re-apply edge fades to imported clips.

Adding takes three steps:

  1. Add the key to SoundBank.UsedKeys. This is what LoadPlaceholderClips iterates, so a key that is not in the list is never loaded from Resources.
  2. Optionally add a matching description at the same index in SoundBank.Palette. SourceOf tolerates a short palette, but keeping the two arrays aligned is the point of the file.
  3. Ship Resources/Audio/<key>.wav (or .ogg) and call it:
SoundDirector.Sfx("bell", 0.8f, 1.1f);

If the file is missing, the key still exists in the dictionary only if BuildClips made one — a brand new key with no synth clip and no file will be silently skipped by Play. For a new key without a resource, either write a Make entry in BuildClips or accept the silence until the asset lands.

Keep the key list stable

The 21 names are referenced by string across combat, the hub and the UI. Renaming a key means finding every Sfx("…") call; adding keys is cheap, renaming them is not.

docs.title: Building the Harvesthold
docs.text:
Every permanent improvement in Chosen of the Harvest is a sanctum: a billboard placed on a one-metre grid around the hub altar. Sanctums produce food, wood, stone, herbs, grace and pearls; they house workers and sleepers; and their auras quiet or radicalise the companions standing nearby. This page covers the build menu, placement rules, all twenty sanctum types, the condition and dirt model, worker hauling, and the small interior grid you can decorate.

Two keys, one system

B opens the build menu in the hub and the interior menu inside a building. K opens the cross-system catalog, which lists every sanctum with its cost and effect without entering placement mode.

docs.title: Placing a sanctum
docs.text:
ShowBuildMenu pages through SanctumType five entries at a time; choosing one calls BeginPlacement. Placement is a separate input mode: the game locks movement, spawns a translucent ghost, and waits for you to commit.

Input Action W A S D Move the ghost one metre at a time Q Rotate a quarter turn (cosmetic flip) E or Space Confirm Esc Cancel and refund nothing, because nothing was spent

The ghost is green when the spot is legal and affordable, red otherwise. Four rules decide legality:

if (Mathf.Abs(position.x) > hubBounds.x - 1.5f ||
    Mathf.Abs(position.z) > hubBounds.y - 1.5f)
    return false;

foreach (var building in buildings)
{
    if (building == null || building == ignore) continue;
    if (Vector3.Distance(position, building.transform.position) < 2.4f) return false;
}

The remaining checks reject the statue, altar, portal, NPC, gathering nodes and the player's own body. Moving an existing sanctum uses the same ghost and the same checks, but skips the affordability test — relocating is free, and workers and sleepers are re-bound to the new spot on confirmation.

The hub box is tighter than the walkable box

You can walk to about ±19 by ±14, but placement is limited to the hub bounds minus 1.5 m. A sanctum also keeps 2.4 m of clear ground around it, so a dense row of farms is not possible. Plan lanes, not clusters.

docs.title: The twenty sanctums
docs.text:
Costs are charged in wood and stone at placement. Aura is the radius in metres inside which the building's continuous effect applies; — means no aura.

Sanctum Wood Stone Height Aura Effect Worker Farm 20 0 1.8 — +2 food / 12 s Yes Shrine 0 25 2.6 4.2 +1 grace / 8 s, scaled by dirt Yes Bed 15 0 1.6 — A sleeping spot for one companion No Lumberyard 30 0 2.8 — +1 wood / 10 s Yes Quarry 20 20 2.2 — +1 stone / 12 s Yes Kitchen 25 10 2.0 — 2 food → 1 meal / 16 s Yes Storage 30 10 1.7 — Raises every resource cap No Herb garden 20 0 1.8 — +1 herb / 14 s Yes Apothecary 30 20 2.0 — 2 herbs → 1 medicine / 18 s Yes Tea house 30 10 2.1 5.2 Companions socialise farther No Memorial 25 10 2.2 3.2 Holds memorials for the dead No Reflection 40 20 2.0 — Confines a dissenter until loyalty returns No Sun bath 25 15 2.2 4.5 Nearby companions rest and recover loyalty No Obelisk 15 30 2.6 5.5 +1 grace / 12 s and a wide loyalty aura No Temple 50 30 2.8 6.0 +2 grace / 12 s and a loyalty aura No Sawmill 35 10 2.7 — +2 wood / 9 s Yes Stoneworks 30 20 2.3 — +2 stone / 10 s Yes Wheat field 25 5 1.9 — +2 food / 10 s Yes Bell tower 40 35 2.9 7.0 +1 grace / 15 s and the widest aura No Reliquary 30 25 2.1 3.5 +1 pearl / 18 s and a small loyalty aura No

The label you see is localised, so the herb garden is "Herb Terrace", the farm is "Rose Garden" and the temple is the "Grand Temple" in English. Sanctum.Label looks up building.<type> in the lexicon and falls back to the raw enum name.

docs.title: Production, in detail
docs.text:
Production is timer-based and checked in Sanctum.Update. Each cycle adds an amount to the building's internal Stored buffer, which you collect by pressing R on the building. The buffer's capacity is:

int capacity = Capacity + bonus * 4 + levelBonus * 4;

Capacity is 10, bonus is the worker's WorkBonus and levelBonus is Level - 1. A level-3 building with a skilled worker therefore buffers 22 units before it stops producing — enough to leave running while you are in the Fallow.

Sanctum Interval Base yield Per worker point Per level Farm 12 s 2 food +1 +1 Lumberyard 10 s 1 wood +1 +1 Quarry 12 s 1 stone +1 +1 Herb garden 14 s 1 herb +1 +1 Sawmill 9 s 2 wood +1 +1 Stoneworks 10 s 2 stone +1 +1 Wheat field 10 s 2 food +1 +1 Shrine 8 s 1 grace +1 +1 Kitchen 16 s 2 food → 1 meal — — Apothecary 18 s 2 herbs → 1 medicine — — Obelisk 12 s 1 grace — — Temple 12 s 2 grace — — Bell tower 15 s 1 grace — — Reliquary 18 s 1 pearl — —

Shrines and the four grace buildings are the exception to the Stored model: they credit grace directly and pop a floating "+1 grace" over the roof, so there is nothing to collect. Farms and wheat fields add HarvestState.BonusFood at collection time, which is how the Harvest creed and the Wheel omen turn a 2-food cycle into a 3-food cycle.

Workers are multipliers, not requirements

Only the kitchen and apothecary refuse to run without a worker. Every other producer keeps ticking at its base rate, so an unstaffed farm is slow, not dead. Assigning a worker to a farm is usually a better return than building a second farm, because the worker adds to yield and capacity.

docs.title: Condition and dirt
docs.text:
Sanctums wear out. Update subtracts 0.04 condition per second from every building, which is 100 condition in roughly 42 minutes of real time. Condition scales output linearly from 0.55× at zero to 1× at full:

float conditionScale = Mathf.Lerp(0.55f, 1f, Condition / 100f);

Nothing stops producing at zero condition; it simply produces at 55%. Repair is priced from the missing condition, not the building's cost:

Cost Formula Wood max(1, ceil((100 − condition) × 0.12)) Stone max(1, ceil((100 − condition) × 0.08))

A building at 50% costs 6 wood and 4 stone; a building at 12% costs 11 wood and 8 stone. Repair always restores to 100, never partially, and the menu refuses when condition is already above 99.5.

Shrines have a second axis. They accumulate dirt at 0.25 per second, and grace output is multiplied by Mathf.Lerp(1f, 0.35f, Dirt / 100f) — a fully filthy shrine produces about a third of its listed grace. Companions on cleaning duty scrub 12 dirt per second, and they will pick a shrine automatically when it is the dirtiest thing in the hold.

docs.title: Managing a sanctum
docs.text:
Pressing R at a building opens a six-entry menu. The header shows its label, level and condition.

Entry Cost Result Move Free Re-enters placement with the building hidden Upgrade round(cost × 0.6) + 10 wood, round(cost × 0.6) + 8 stone +1 level, max 3 Remove Refunds half the base wood and stone Deletes the sanctum and unassigns staff Collect / Craft / Stores / Release Free Context action for that type Repair See above Restores condition to 100 Enter interior Free Switches to the 7 × 5 interior grid

Upgrading is intentionally cheaper than rebuilding: a Farm upgrade costs 22 wood and 8 stone, while a second Farm costs 20 wood and occupies new ground. The trade is space against throughput, and it is the main reason vertical specialisation beats sprawl in a mature hold.

Removing a building is not destructive to companions. RemoveSanctum releases any penitent, clears the worker's job, unassigns the sleeper, refunds half the cost, and then re-runs worker and bed assignment for the whole roster.

docs.title: Workers, sleepers and hauling
docs.text:
TryAssignWorker walks the companion list and gives an unemployed, able companion the first job that needs one. The NeedsWorker set is farm, lumberyard, quarry, shrine, kitchen, herb garden, apothecary, sawmill, stoneworks and wheat field. A companion cannot work while sick, dissenting or confined.

Production is not the only labour. A worker whose buffer reaches four units (two for an herb garden) picks the load up and carries it to the hold's deposit point:

if (Job != null && Job.Stored >= (Job.Type == SanctumType.HerbGarden ? 2 : 4))
    StartHaul();

HaulSpot is the storage building's front edge if one exists, otherwise the altar. On arrival, DepositHaul credits the resources and the worker walks back. FlushHaul deposits anything in hand before a save or a forced task change, so resources are never silently lost when you reassign someone mid-carry.

docs.title: Storage and caps
docs.text:
Storage is the only building whose effect is global. Each level adds to every cap, and HarvestState.NotifyChanged clamps all eight resources after every change, so overflow is impossible.

Resource Base cap Per storage level Wood 250 +100 Stone 250 +100 Food 100 +50 Herbs 30 +20 Meals 30 +20 Medicine 10 +5 Bombs 5 +2 Potions 20 +0

Bombs also gain +2 from the Magician omen and +2 from the Lantern heirloom; potions gain +5 from the Hermit omen. Those bonuses apply whether or not you own a storage, but the storage multiplier is what makes a bomb-heavy run practical.

docs.title: Bell tower, temple and the loyalty auras
docs.text:
Auras are checked once per frame per companion in FollowerAgent. They are small, continuous drips rather than bursts, and they stack only in the sense that a companion standing in two auras gets both.

Building Per-second effect inside the aura Shrine +0.018 loyalty Tea house +0.01 loyalty Sun bath +0.01 loyalty, −0.08 exhaustion Obelisk Loyalty aura, plus grace production Temple Loyalty aura, plus grace production Bell tower Loyalty aura, plus grace production Reliquary Small loyalty aura, plus pearls

The Tea House is the social building: its 5.2 m radius lets companions find conversation partners farther apart, which is what drives friendship and romance checks. The Sun Bath is the recovery building: it burns exhaustion while adding loyalty, making it the pair to a workshop district.

docs.title: Interiors
docs.text:
Choosing Enter interior hides the hub and builds a small room around you. The floor is 8.2 m across, movement is bounded to ±3.6 by ±3.1, and the camera pulls in to 8.2. The buildable grid is 7 columns by 5 rows:

static Vector2Int InteriorCell(Vector3 position) =>
    new Vector2Int(
        Mathf.Clamp(Mathf.RoundToInt(position.x), -3, 3),
        Mathf.Clamp(Mathf.RoundToInt(position.z), -2, 2));

Pieces are placed on the cell you are standing on, and an occupied cell is refused. Costs are deliberately small:

Piece Cost Notes Wall 5 wood Solid; blocks movement Door 10 wood Walk-through, the exit prompt Candle 3 pearls Decoration; +0.6 aura to the parent sanctum

Each candle permanently raises InteriorAuraBonus on the sanctum by 0.6 m, and removing one lowers it again. That is the only way to grow an aura beyond its base radius, and it applies to whichever aura the building already has — a bell tower with three candles projects 8.8 m instead of 7.

Interiors are saved, not rebuilt from a template

Every piece is written into SanctumData.interior as a type, x, z triple. BuildInterior replays that list on load. Removing a piece removes its entry and its aura bonus, so a save always matches what you see.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
Sanctum (Scripts/Buildings/Building.cs) is a plain MonoBehaviour with no ScriptableObject backing. The type, level, stored amount, dirt, condition and three companion references are public fields; costs and aura radii are static switch expressions on the type.

HarvestGame owns the list of placed sanctums and mirrors it into HarvestState.Data.buildings as SanctumData records for saving. The two lists are index-aligned, which is why moving or removing a building has to update both in the same method — see ConfirmPlacement and RemoveSanctum.

Placement validity is deliberately geometric rather than physics-based:

bool geometry = IsPlacementValid(placementType, placementCursor, placementMoving);
bool affordable = placementMoving != null ||
                  (HarvestState.Data.wood >= Sanctum.CostWood(placementType) &&
                   HarvestState.Data.stone >= Sanctum.CostStone(placementType));

There is no overlap test against gathering nodes or companions inside IsPlacementValid itself; those checks run earlier in the same method, before the distance loop, so keep them together if you extend the rule set.

RebuildNavGrid runs after every placement, move and removal. Companions use a coarse grid rather than a navmesh, so a wall placed across the middle of the hold can genuinely trap someone until the next rebuild — which is exactly what happens, because the rebuild is triggered by the placement, not by the trapped companion.

docs.title: Ceremonies & omens
docs.text: Ceremonies are the ritual layer that ties the settlement economy to progression. Omens are run-altering modifiers collected from bosses and chests.

docs.title: Ceremonies
docs.text:
Open the ceremony menu at the Harvest Altar and choose with 1–6. The altar has a short cooldown between ceremonies (HarvestAltar.CanPreach).

# Ceremony Cost Effect 1 Hymn 1 food per companion Grace scaled by attendance, hunger, traits, sickness and dissent; +3 loyalty and +15 XP per companion 2 Feast 8 food (4 with a Kitchen) +20 grace (× grace multiplier), feeds everyone, +10 loyalty, +8 XP 3 Sacrifice 1 companion (requires more than 3) +45 grace, +10 pearls 4 Sharpen blade 15 pearls +5 permanent weapon damage 5 Ceremony of Plenty 10 food +5 meals, +10 grace 6 Ceremony of Warding 10 pearls Cures and strengthens every companion

docs.title: How the hymn payout is calculated
docs.text:
The hymn is deliberately the most legible ceremony, and the one worth tuning first.

int baseGain = 5;
foreach (var f in companions)
{
    if (f.Hunger < 30f) { hungry++; baseGain += 1; }
    else baseGain += 2;

    baseGain += f.GraceBonus;                 // Devout trait
    if (f.Sick) baseGain -= 1;
    if (f.Dissenter) baseGain -= 2;
}

int fed = Mathf.Min(HarvestState.Data.food, HarvestState.Data.companions);
HarvestState.Data.food -= fed;
float penalty = fed < HarvestState.Data.companions ? 0.5f : 1f;
int gain = Mathf.RoundToInt(baseGain * HarvestState.GraceMultiplier * penalty);

So a well-fed, devout, healthy flock is worth roughly three times a starving, sick, dissenting one. The GraceMultiplier comes from creeds, omens and heirlooms.

docs.title: Creeds
docs.text: Every third hymn, OfferCreed presents a one-time choice of creed. Creeds are stored as three separate slots — grace, combat, economy — and apply passive bonuses from HarvestState (GraceMultiplier, BonusDamage, GatherBonus, BonusPearls, BonusFood).

docs.title: Cooldown and interruption
docs.text: CeremonyRoutine locks input, gathers companions at the altar, waits 3.4 seconds, applies the effect, waits 1.6 seconds, then releases everyone. Nothing else can start while ceremonyRunning is true, and saving is blocked.

docs.title: Omens
docs.text:
Omens are collected after boss fights and from chests. Each is a permanent modifier for the current save. The deck has 18 entries:

Id Omen Effect sun Dawnfire +15 maximum health moon Shrouded Tides +15% grace from ceremonies star Lodestar +5 melee damage tower Shattered Spire +1 pearl per slain husk wheel Turning Garden +1 food per Rose Garden harvest death Last Petal +10% weapon damage judgement Rite of Rebirth Rites recharge 25% faster temperance Still Pool Heal 8 after every cleared room devil Thorned Crown +12% critical chance and stronger crits hermit Lantern Keeper +5 potion capacity hanged Suspended Bloom +15% rite damage world Worldroot +10% grace from ceremonies priestess Harvest Oracle +10 maximum health emperor Sovereign's Seal +2 melee damage empress Harvest Empress +1 food per Rose Garden harvest chariot Swift Chariot +5% movement speed magician Ember Magician +2 bomb capacity lovers Twin Blossoms +5 maximum health

The deck lives in one array in GameBootstrap.cs:

static readonly (string id, string name, string desc)[] OmenDeck =
{
    ("sun", "Dawnfire", "+15 maximum health"),
    // ...
};

Adding an omen means adding a tuple and checking HarvestState.HasOmen(id) wherever the effect should apply.

docs.title: Heirlooms and attire
docs.text:
Two more permanent layers sit alongside omens:

  • 18 heirlooms (HeirloomCatalog) — permanent passives bought in shops or found in chests. All owned heirlooms apply at once.
  • 11 attire pieces (AttireCatalog) — split into Armor and Charm slots. One of each is equipped at a time; HarvestState.DamageTakenMultiplier, RiteCooldownMultiplier and friends read the equipped ids.
Armor Effect Charm Effect Rose Mantle +12 max health Cinder Charm +12% weapon damage Sun Scale −10% damage taken Tideglass Charm Rites recharge 20% faster Thorn Mail Attackers take 4 damage Fang Charm Attacks 8% faster Pearl Plate +15 max health Owl Pinion +5% crit chance Guardian Sigil −5% damage taken Serpent Coil Melee hits heal 1 Silver Mantle Rites recharge 10% faster

docs.title: Combat in the Fallow
docs.text:
Combat in Chosen of the Harvest is built from four verbs — swing, dodge, cast and throw — layered over a fixed list of armaments, rites and husk archetypes. Every number below comes from the same handful of classes, so the feel of a run is the sum of your loadout, your omens and heirlooms, and the act you chose. This page covers the controls, the damage formulas, every creature family, and the three wardens waiting at the end of each act.

The four verbs

Space attacks with the equipped armament, Left Shift rolls, X casts the equipped rite and G throws a bomb. All four are rebindable in settings; the defaults live in Bindings.Defaults (Scripts/Core/Controls.cs).

docs.title: Controls and the shape of a fight
docs.text:
A fight is deliberately readable. Husks telegraph with a red ground ring before they strike, your own swings lunge you a short distance forward, and the dodge roll grants more invulnerability than it consumes in time. The result is a loop of commit, read, roll, punish.

Input Default Behaviour Attack Space Swings the current armament; combos chain inside ComboWindow Dodge Left Shift 0.22 s roll at 11 m/s, 0.42 s of i-frames, 0.75 s cooldown Rite X Radial burst centred on the player Bomb G Lobs a bomb 3.4 m ahead; 0.9 s cooldown, consumes one bomb Potion H Drinks a potion from the inventory Interact E Doors, chests, altars, the portal

The player's own hurtbox is generous in your favour: after taking a hit you get 0.7 s of invulnerability, so overlapping husks cannot chain-stun you to death.

docs.title: Armaments
docs.text:
Twelve armaments are defined in ArmamentCatalog. They are not sidegrades with different skins — each changes range, arc, knockback, combo count and status application. HarvestState.Data.weaponType stores the equipped id, and the armory in the hub cycles through them.

Armament Damage Cooldown Range Combo Notable property Rose Saber 25 0.34 s 1.9 3 Baseline; balanced arc Golden Axe 42 0.58 s 2.05 1 Slow 0.55× for 1.3 s, heavy knockback Fan Blade 13 0.19 s 1.45 4 Bleed 3 dps for 3.5 s Silk Lance 30 0.42 s 2.65 2 Longest reach of the light weapons Bell Hammer 52 0.88 s 2.15 1 Hits all around; slow 0.45× for 1.6 s Thorn Claws 9 0.14 s 1.25 5 1 lifesteal per hit Crescent Scythe 36 0.5 s 2.5 2 Bleed 2 dps for 3 s, wide arc Sunburst Mace 58 1.0 s 2.0 1 Hits all; slow 0.4× for 2 s Chain of Petals 38 0.72 s 2.35 2 Hits all; slow 0.5× for 1.4 s Glass Rapier 20 0.22 s 2.2 4 Long lunge (0.42), narrow arc Jade Cleaver 46 0.66 s 1.85 2 Bleed 5 dps for 4 s Royal Halberd 40 0.55 s 2.8 2 Longest reach overall

HitsAll weapons skip the facing check entirely — the Bell Hammer, Sunburst Mace and Chain of Petals hit every husk inside Range. Everything else compares Vector3.Dot(facingDir, direction) against the weapon's ArcDot, so a negative value like the axe's -0.05 still covers a wide cone.

The combo bonus is per swing, not per enemy

Combo index increments once per attack and resets after ComboWindow elapses. Each step adds 15% damage to every husk hit by that swing.

docs.title: Damage, in full
docs.text:
PlayerController.Attack() builds the final number from the equipped armament, your progression and your relics:

bool critical = UnityEngine.Random.value < HarvestState.CriticalChance;
int damage = Mathf.RoundToInt(HarvestState.WeaponDamage * (1f + comboIndex * 0.15f) *
    (critical ? HarvestState.CriticalMultiplier : 1f));

HarvestState.WeaponDamage is the other half of the story:

int damage = ArmamentCatalog.Current.BaseDamage + BonusDamage + Data.weaponLevel * 5 +
             (HasOmen("star") ? 5 : 0) + (HasOmen("emperor") ? 2 : 0) +
             Data.metaWrath * 4 + (HasHeirloom("fang") ? 5 : 0);
float multiplier = (Data.charmId == "ember" ? 1.12f : 1f) *
                   (HasOmen("death") ? 1.1f : 1f);
return Mathf.RoundToInt(damage * multiplier);

Criticals start at 8% and 1.6×, and several items move both figures. On the receiving end, Creature.Hit applies flat reduction first (the Mirror Sentinel has 20%, Armored elites 30%), and PlayerController.TakeDamage applies your own mitigation last:

damage = Mathf.Max(1, Mathf.RoundToInt(
    damage * HarvestState.DamageTakenMultiplier * Preferences.IncomingDamageMultiplier));

The Mathf.Max(1, ...) is load-bearing: no stack of armour can make you literally immune to a hit.

docs.title: Rites
docs.text:
Rites are radial, instant, and independent of your armament. All three are unlocked from the start so the combat sandbox can be tested end to end, and the ritual menu cycles between them.

Rite Damage Radius Cooldown Extra effect Sunburst 34 3.5 7.5 s Strong knockback (4.5) Shroud of Frost 18 4.1 8.5 s Slow 0.42× for 2.8 s Crimson Vow 22 3.2 9.5 s Heals 5 per husk hit

Rite damage adds a third of your Wrath meta upgrade, then multiplies:

int damage = Mathf.Max(1, Mathf.RoundToInt(
    (rite.Damage + HarvestState.Data.metaWrath * 3) * HarvestState.RiteDamageMultiplier));

Cooldowns are multiplied by RiteCooldownMultiplier, which the Tide charm (0.8×), Moon armour (0.9×), the Judgement omen (0.75×) and the Bell heirloom (0.9×) all reduce. A fully stacked rite build casts roughly twice as often as a bare one. Hits are counted for the floating text and for Crimson Vow's healing, so a rite into a packed room is worth far more than its listed damage.

docs.title: Bombs
docs.text:
Bombs are consumables, not a cooldown ability. ThrowBomb refuses to fire at zero stock and points you at the apothecary; otherwise it spends one, waits 0.9 s, and lobs the bomb at a point 3.4 m ahead.

Property Value Direct damage 30 + metaWrath × 2 Blast radius 2.4 Burn 3 s at 4 dps Knockback 5 Cooldown 0.9 s

Bombs ignore the facing cone, so they are the answer to a room that has already surrounded you. The burn ticks every half second like every other damage-over-time effect.

docs.title: Status effects
docs.text:
Creature tracks four timed effects and ticks them all through one method. Applications take the stronger value rather than stacking, so re-applying a weaker bleed never overwrites a stronger one.

Status Applied by Tick Bleed Fan Blade, Crescent Scythe, Jade Cleaver 0.5 s, ceil(dps × 0.5) Burn Bombs 0.5 s Poison Cinder husks and dungeon hazards 0.5 s Slow Axe, hammer, mace, flail, Shroud of Frost Continuous factor, clamped 0.25–1 
public void ApplyBleed(float duration, float dps)
{
    if (dead) return;
    bleedTime = Mathf.Max(bleedTime, duration);
    bleedDps = Mathf.Max(bleedDps, dps);
}

Because duration and dps are each maxed independently, a weak long bleed and a strong short bleed combine into a strong long one. That is intentional: it makes mixed parties feel better than the sum of their parts.

docs.title: Creature archetypes
docs.text:
Every husk is a Creature with an Archetype. The archetype sets speed, attack range and attack cooldown at spawn, and chooses which brain runs in Update. The twelve families are:

Archetype In-game name Speed Range Cooldown Behaviour Melee Thornbound Duelist 2.3 1.05 1.1 s Balanced chaser Fast Silk Wisp 3.15 0.95 0.85 s Fragile rusher Brute Rootbound Ogre 1.65 1.35 1.45 s Slow heavy hitter Caster Moth Seer 2.0 1.05 1.3 s Keeps 3.1–6.4 m, fires bolts Charger Briar Hound 2.5 1.0 1.2 s Wind-up then long dash Exploder Cinder Husk 2.9 0.9 1.0 s Detonates on death Shielder Mirror Sentinel 1.5 1.2 1.7 s 20% damage reduction Summoner Fallow Choir 2.1 1.05 1.6 s Summons capped minions Healer Verdant Mender 2.3 1.05 1.5 s Heals nearby husks Archer Glass Archer 2.5 1.05 1.5 s Long-range rapid bolts Slammer Bell Golem 1.6 1.7 2.1 s Telegraphed radial shockwave Assassin Shroud Stalker 3.35 1.0 0.9 s Blinks behind the Sovereign

The brains differ in more than stats. The Archer fires every 1.7 s and keeps a 4.5–8.5 m band; the Caster fires every 2.5 s and prefers 3.1–6.4 m. The Summoner retreats below 4.2 m and advances past 7 m, summoning on a 4–7 s timer. The Healer holds 4–8 m and heals allies on a 3.5–6 s timer. The Slammer winds up for 0.55 s and deals 1.2× damage in a 2.8 m radius. The Assassin blinks to a random point within 1.6 m of you and resets its attack timer on arrival.

Elites are modifiers, not archetypes

An elite keeps its base brain and adds one of three modifiers: Armored (30% reduction), Frenzied (+25% speed, ×0.8 cooldown) or Vampiric (heals 30% of damage dealt). A Vampiric Brute is a very different problem from a Vampiric Wisp.

docs.title: The three wardens
docs.text:
Each act ends in a WardenController layered over a regular Creature. The warden flips to phase two at 50% health, shortening its telegraphs and adding radial volleys. Arenas are dressed by WardenArena but share the same collision and room graph.

Act Warden Arena theme Moveset 0 The Gilded Stag Gilded Court Antler charge, antler volley, slam 1 The Mire Queen Drowned Ring Thorn snare, mire fan, slam 2 The Obsidian Sultan Obsidian Court Mirage surge, teleport, radial bolts

The shared slam is the backbone of all three fights:

float radius = phase == 1 ? 2.8f : 3.5f;
float duration = phase == 1 ? 0.8f : 0.55f;
...
pc.TakeDamage(phase == 1 ? 18 : 24);

Phase two also changes the follow-up. The Stag fires 8 radial bolts (11 damage, 4.4 m/s); the Mire Queen fires 11 green bolts and a 5-bolt fan; the Sultan fires 14 blue bolts and teleports next to you. Attack timers shorten from 3.0 s to 2.0 s for acts 0 and 1, and from 2.4 s to 1.5 s for act 2 — the Sultan is relentless by design.

Roll through, not away

Every warden attack is a ground-centred radius or a slow projectile. The dodge's 0.42 s of i-frames is longer than the 0.55 s phase-two slam telegraph only if you start rolling late. Rolling early leaves you standing in the ring when it lands.

docs.title: Difficulty
docs.text:
Difficulty is a persisted preference, not a per-run choice. It scales incoming damage and creature health, and nothing else — enemy damage, speed and loot stay identical.

Setting Incoming damage Creature health Easy 0.7× 0.85× Normal 1.0× 1.0× Hard 1.3× 1.2× 
public static float IncomingDamageMultiplier => Difficulty switch
{
    0 => 0.7f,
    2 => 1.3f,
    _ => 1f
};

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
Combat lives in three files. PlayerController owns the four verbs, their cooldowns and the hurtbox. Creature owns every husk's brain, status timers and death. WardenController owns the two-phase boss script.

Creature.Init is where an archetype becomes a stat block. It reads Preferences.CreatureHealthMultiplier once, so difficulty is baked in at spawn rather than applied per hit:

MaxHealth = Mathf.Max(1, Mathf.RoundToInt(health * Preferences.CreatureHealthMultiplier));
Health = MaxHealth;
Damage = Mathf.Max(1, damage);
IsWarden = boss;
Kind = kind;
Phase = 1;

The brains are plain distance switches in Update. There is no behaviour tree, no navmesh and no steering beyond Move(direction), which resolves against RoomCollision and slides along walls when blocked. That is why husks can be baited around pillars reliably — the slide is geometric, not pathfound.

Damage flows one way: PlayerController.Attack calls Creature.Hit, which applies reduction and calls Die() at zero. Die() is also where the Exploder's detonation, the loot roll and the room-clear check happen, so killing a Cinder Husk in a doorway can still hurt you after the room is technically empty.

Creature.All is a static list maintained in OnEnable/OnDisable. Every ability iterates a snapshot (.ToArray()) because a husk can die mid-loop and remove itself. If you add a new area attack, do the same or you will hit InvalidOperationException on the first kill.

The dodge is worth reading in full, because its numbers are the whole defensive game:

dodgeDir = moveInput.sqrMagnitude > 0.01f ? moveInput.normalized : facingDir;
dodgeTimer = 0.22f;
dodgeCooldown = 0.75f;
invuln = Mathf.Max(invuln, 0.42f);

invuln is shared with the post-hit grace period, and Mathf.Max means a dodge can extend existing i-frames but never shorten them. Chaining a dodge directly after a hit therefore gives you 0.42 s from the moment of the roll, not 0.7 s plus 0.42 s.

docs.text: The Harvesthold runs on twelve tracked resources. Every producer, cost and cap lives in code, so tuning the economy is a matter of editing a constant.

docs.title: Storage caps
docs.text:
Caps are enforced centrally in HarvestState.NotifyChanged, so every producer obeys them automatically.

Resource Cap Wood 250 + storageLevels × 100 Stone 250 + storageLevels × 100 Food 100 + storageLevels × 50 Herbs 30 + storageLevels × 20 Meals 30 + storageLevels × 20 Medicine 10 + storageLevels × 5 Bombs 5 + storageLevels × 2 + omen/heirloom bonuses Potions 20 + 5 if the Lantern Keeper omen is held

storageLevels is the sum of the levels of every Vault (Storage) sanctum. That makes storage the one building that scales indefinitely in value.

// GameState.cs
public static int StorageLevels
{
    get
    {
        int levels = 0;
        foreach (var building in Data.buildings)
            if (string.Equals(building.type, "Storage", StringComparison.Ordinal))
                levels += Mathf.Max(1, building.level);
        return levels;
    }
}

docs.title: Production
docs.text:
Producing sanctums accumulate output on a timer and store up to 10 units before they stop. A worker assigned to the sanctum is required for the listed interval; without one the rate is slower.

Sanctum Output Interval Rose Garden (Farm) Food 12 s Sunwell (Shrine) Grace 8 s Timber Grove (Lumberyard) Wood 10 s Marble Quarry (Quarry) Stone 12 s Kitchen Pavilion Meals 16 s Herb Terrace Herbs 14 s Elixir Atelier (Apothecary) Medicine, potions 18 s Timber Mill (Sawmill) Wood 9 s Stoneworks Stone 10 s Wheat Field Food 10 s Bell Tower Grace 15 s Reliquary Pearls 18 s

Auto-haul

Companions with the hauling job collect from producing sanctums and deposit into storage automatically. Manual collection (E on the building) is always faster but costs your attention.

docs.title: Food and meals
docs.text:
Feeding is the core pressure on the economy.

  • A hymn feeds one food per companion (up to the number of companions). If there is not enough food, the grace gain is halved.
  • A feast feeds everyone and grants +10 loyalty each. It costs 8 food, or 4 if you have built a Kitchen Pavilion.
  • Meals are the efficient food unit: a meal feeds a companion without consuming raw food. MealCap limits how many you can stockpile.

docs.title: Pearls
docs.text:
Pearls are the combat currency. They come from kills, chests, boss rewards and the Sacrifice ceremony. They are spent on:

  • Sharpen blade — 15 pearls for +5 permanent weapon damage (repeatable);
  • Ceremony of Warding — 10 pearls to cure and strengthen everyone;
  • shop stock during expeditions.

Because sharpening is unlimited, pearls are the main long-run power sink. If you rebalance the economy, change the pearl drop rate and the sharpen cost together.

docs.title: Devotion
docs.text:
Devotion is the meta-currency. It survives death and is spent on permanent upgrades from the pilgrimage map.

Upgrade Effect Vitality +15 maximum health Wrath +4 damage Provisions +10 food and +5 meals immediately Charisma New companions start with +3 loyalty

Devotion is earned from:

  • quest completion (2 devotion per early stage, 4 per late stage);
  • boss kills (8 / 12 / 16 by act);
  • pilgrimages;
  • the Sovereign's Diadem heirloom (+15% devotion from pilgrimages).

docs.title: Shop rooms
docs.text: Expeditions contain shop rooms where pearls buy heirlooms and attire. Stock is drawn from HeirloomCatalog.RandomUnowned() and AttireCatalog.RandomUnowned(), so once everything is owned, shops stop offering gear and become pearl sinks for consumables.

docs.title: Expeditions into the Fallow
docs.text:
The Fallow is the template's roguelike half. It is entered through the portal in the Harvesthold, it is generated one room at a time from a fixed act budget, and it is the only place where pearls, omens and heirlooms come from. This page covers the curse roll, the floor graph, every room type, keys and corridors, the act pacing, and how a run ends.

A run is a snapshot

The Fallow is not a separate scene. EnterExpedition disables hubRoot, resets your health, rolls a curse, and hands control to Expedition.Begin. When you leave, ExitExpedition re-enables the hub at the exact position you left from — building timers and companion needs resume where they stopped.

docs.title: Entering the portal
docs.text:
Standing at the portal and pressing E opens ShowCampaignMap(), not the dungeon. The map lists three acts plus Devotion upgrades and Quest log. An act that is ahead of campaignStage is refused with "Clear the previous warden first". Choosing an available act shows an intro card, and only its Begin pilgrimage entry calls:

public void EnterExpedition(int act)
{
    if (mode != Mode.Hub || ceremonyRunning) return;

    currentAct = Mathf.Clamp(act, 0, 2);
    HarvestState.RollCurse();
    mode = Mode.Expedition;
    hubReturnPosition = Player.transform.position;
    hubRoot.SetActive(false);

    Audio.Play("portal", 0.8f);
    Audio.PlayMusic("music_dungeon");
    ...
    HarvestState.Data.pilgrimages++;
    Player.SetHealth(Player.MaxHealth);
    ExpeditionRef.Begin(this, currentAct);
}

pilgrimages is not cosmetic: it is the depth scalar used by chest pearls, trap damage, and every husk's health and damage formula.

docs.title: Curses rolled on entry
docs.text:
HarvestState.RollCurse() picks uniformly from the three real curses — it can never return Curse.None:

Curse Effect Where it is applied Fury +30% enemy damage Creature.DamageMultiplier at spawn Frailty −25 maximum health RunHealthPenalty, subtracted in MaxHealth Gloom +25% enemy speed Creature.SpeedMultiplier at spawn

The curse is runtime-only (HarvestState.CurrentCurse) and is cleared by ClearRunState() on exit, so it never leaks into a save. It is printed in the HUD status line next to the husk count.

docs.title: Act structure
docs.text:
Three acts, two floors each, six floors in total. Each floor is regenerated from scratch, so the graph is different every descent.

Act Biome Warden Floor grid Rooms per floor Rooms per act 0 Ashen Orchard The Gilded Stag 5 × 2 10 20 1 Drowned Conservatory The Mire Queen 8 × 2 16 32 2 Ember Citadel The Obsidian Sultan 5 × 4 20 40

JourneyPacing (Scripts/Core/CampaignPacing.cs) states the same budget as constants and adds the intended session length:

Constant Value ActOneRooms 20 ActTwoRooms 32 ActThreeRooms 40 TotalRooms 92 TargetMinutesMin / Max 80 / 120 Summary 92 rooms • 80-120 min target

The warden reward budget is 8 / 12 / 16 devotion, which WardenDefeated computes as 8 + act * 4 before the crown heirloom multiplier.

docs.title: How a floor is generated
docs.text:
FloorPlanGenerator.Generate(act, out lockedEdges) builds the whole graph before the first room is drawn. It lays out a rectangular grid, connects every room to its right and lower neighbour (so every room is reachable), marks rooms[0] as the entrance and the last room as the warden, then distributes role rooms into the middle.

int columns = act switch { 1 => 8, 2 => 5, _ => 5 };
int rows = act == 2 ? 4 : 2;
int bossId = columns * rows - 1;
...
var roles = new List<RoomType>
{
    RoomType.Shop, RoomType.Treasure, RoomType.Curse,
    RoomType.Puzzle, RoomType.Rescue, RoomType.Forge
};
int elites = 1 + act;
for (int i = 0; i < elites; i++) roles.Add(RoomType.Elite);
if (act >= 1) roles.Add(RoomType.Treasure);

The role list is shuffled, then written into consecutive room ids from 1 upwards; anything left before the warden becomes a plain Combat room. That guarantees every utility room appears at least once per floor, with one elite in act one, two in act two and three in act three, plus a second treasure room from act two.

Finally it locks Mathf.Min(2 + act, candidates.Count) edges between ordinary rooms — never an edge touching the entrance or the warden — and returns them as packed EdgeKey(a, b) integers. Those become the locked doors.

docs.title: Room types
docs.text:
RoomType has ten members. FloorPlanGenerator.Name localises them through the room.* lexicon keys.

Room Objective What is inside Entrance none Spawn room; doors open immediately Combat clear the room 4 husks, doors open at zero Elite defeat the elite 5 husks, one carries an elite modifier, 3 traps Treasure open the chest Chest gives pearls, wood, stone and a key Shop trade, then choose a door Merchant with limited stock and a sell menu Curse touch the altar Take the gift: +1 key, +25 pearls, −20 health Puzzle step on 3 runes Three RunePlate triggers; all three open the doors Rescue free the captive RecruitCompanion(), blocked at the companion cap Forge use the forge Sharpen blade for 15 pearls (+5 damage) Warden slay the warden Boss + two escorts, then a boss chest

Expedition.Update watches Creature.All.Count for combat and elite rooms and calls OpenDoors() the moment the room is empty. There is no wave logic — a summoner that keeps adding minions keeps the room open.

Temperance

The temperance omen heals 8 health on every cleared room except the entrance, and the toast changes to say so. It is one of the strongest sustain picks in the deck; see Ceremonies and omens.

docs.title: Keys, doors and corridors
docs.text:
Keys are a per-floor counter, reset to 0 on every descent. There are three sources: a treasure chest (+1), the merchant (10 pearls), and the cursed altar (+1). Each locked door costs exactly one key and stays unlocked afterwards.

Doors behave in a strict order:

  1. If the room is not cleared, the door refuses and prints the objective.
  2. If the door is locked and you have a key, it consumes the key, recolours itself lilac and stays in place — you must press again.
  3. Otherwise it builds a corridor and moves you into the target room.

A corridor is its own tiny room: RoomHalfWidth = 3.2, RoomHalfDepth = 5.5, no enemies, no chest, one door at the far end. The label above that door names the room type you are about to enter, which is the only preview the game gives you before committing.

docs.title: The pilgrimage map and campaign stages
docs.text:
CampaignStage is Data.campaignStage clamped to 0–3. It is the number of wardens you have broken, and it gates the act list: act 0 is available at stage 0, act 1 at stage 1, act 2 at stage 2. The map also exposes the devotion screen and the quest log.

WardenDefeated(act, bossName) only pays out the first time an act's warden falls:

if (act + 1 > HarvestState.Data.campaignStage)
{
    HarvestState.Data.campaignStage = act + 1;
    int reward = Mathf.RoundToInt((8 + act * 4) *
        (HarvestState.HasHeirloom("crown") ? 1.15f : 1f));
    HarvestState.Data.devotion += reward;
    ...
}

It is called from Expedition.Update only when the warden dies on the last floor (!HasNextFloor), so a first-floor warden kill does not advance the campaign.

docs.title: Descending and finishing
docs.text:
A warden room is the last room of a floor. Killing the warden opens a chest; the chest's omen choice then opens a door labelled DESCEND (or RETURN on the final floor). ExitRun() decides:

Condition Result HasNextFloor BeginNextFloor(): floor++, keys reset, new graph, heal 20% max health last floor Finished = true, boot.ExitExpedition(true)

FloorCount is fixed at 2. The second-floor warden is named with the Ascendant suffix (WardenName appends it when Floor > 1), gets +90 health and +4 damage from floorBonus, and its arena is the same theme as the first floor.

Leaving with loot autosaves if autosave is enabled, and if campaignStage >= 3 and the victory screen has not been seen, ShowVictory() runs once and grants +10 devotion.

docs.title: Dying in the Fallow
docs.text: OnPlayerDied in the expedition branch takes half your pearls, exits the run with loot = false, and wakes you at max(40, MaxHealth / 2). There is no confiscation of wood, stone, heirlooms or omens — pearls are the only death tax.

docs.title: Rewards
Shop rooms
docs.text: ShowShop builds a six-entry merchant menu with per-room stock that resets on every room build: 3 heals, 2 keys, 1 heirloom, 2 potions, 1 attire. The heirloom and attire offers are rolled from RandomUnowned() at room build time, so a shop can never sell you something you already own — and shows "no heirloom to sell" when the catalogue is exhausted. The sell menu trades 10 wood or stone for 8 pearls, 5 food for 6, and 2 herbs for 5.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
The run starts in Expedition.Begin, which clamps the act, fixes the floor count and generates the first graph:

public void Begin(HarvestGame owner, int act)
{
    ActIndex = Mathf.Clamp(act, 0, 2);
    Floor = 1;
    FloorCount = 2;
    BeginRun(owner);
}

Only one room exists at a time. EnterRoom destroys the previous roomRoot, despawns every Creature, resets per-room flags (shopUsed, curseUsed, chest/door/exit state), and rebuilds from the room type. Expedition.End is the mirror image: it despawns enemies, destroys the room and clears RoomCollision, which is why leaving mid-room is safe.

Changing the run length

FloorCount = 2 and the three JourneyPacing room constants are the only places the 6-floor / 92-room budget is expressed. Changing the grid sizes in FloorPlanGenerator.Generate changes the actual rooms per floor, so update both if you want the HUD and the pacing summary to agree.

docs.title: The Harvesthold hub and companions
docs.text:
The Harvesthold is the safe half of Chosen of the Harvest: a 40 by 30 metre ground plane with an altar, a statue, a portal, one talkative NPC and a court of companions who need food, sleep and reasons to stay. You return here after every pilgrimage, and almost every system you touch outside the Fallow — building, ceremonies, the roster — is anchored to a single object in the scene. This page covers the physical layout, the day loop, and the full companion simulation behind the CompanionRecord class.

One class owns the hub

HarvestGame (Scripts/Core/GameBootstrap.cs) builds the hub in Awake() from code — there are no prefabs and no scene references. BuildGround, BuildHarvestAltar, BuildPlayer, BuildResources, BuildCompanions, BuildPortal and BuildNpc run in that order.

docs.title: The hub at a glance
The Harvest Altar
docs.text:
HarvestAltar is deliberately tiny: a radius, a cooldown and a CanPreach gate. Standing inside 3.2 metres and pressing E opens the ceremony menu; MarkUsed() starts a 30-second rest during which the altar refuses every ceremony. Companions physically walk to seats arranged on an ellipse around it before the effect resolves.

See Ceremonies and omens for the five ceremony types and the grace maths.

docs.title: The pilgrimage portal
docs.text:
The portal is a door sprite with a purple glow and a floating PILGRIMAGE label. Interacting with it does not drop you into the Fallow immediately — it opens the pilgrimage map, which lists the three acts, the devotion upgrade screen and the quest log. Choosing an available act shows that act's intro card, and only Begin pilgrimage calls EnterExpedition(act).

The hub keeps running

EnterExpedition deactivates hubRoot rather than unloading the scene, so building timers, companion needs and the day cycle pause while you are in the Fallow. SeasonCycle.Update and Sanctum.Update both early-out on HarvestGame.InputLocked.

docs.title: The Oracle
docs.text:
There is exactly one NPC in the hub. BuildNpc loads Art/Characters/oracle, tints it lavender and hangs a CompanionNameTag reading THE ORACLE. Pressing E within 2.2 metres calls TalkToNpc(), which walks a short intro on the first visit and then hands out one hint per QuestHintKeys entry — build a rose garden, hold a hymn, break the first warden, and so on. The ninth line is the closing speech.

There is no merchant in the hub. The merchant is a dungeon fixture that appears in RoomType.Shop rooms only; see Expeditions.

docs.title: Day and season cycle
docs.text:
SeasonCycle (Scripts/Core/DayCycle.cs) is a four-phase clock: Dawn, Day, Dusk, Night, 60 real seconds each. One full day is therefore four minutes. Each phase repaints Camera.main.backgroundColor; Night is the only phase companions treat as bedtime.

At the transition into Dawn the day counter increments, and HarvestGame runs the nightly bookkeeping:

Step Rule Ageing every companion age++ Old age from age 55, death chance (age - 54) × 1% per day Births TryBirths(), one attempt per dawn Daily event 45% chance of TriggerDailyEvent()

The five daily events are: +6 food, +10 pearls, +8 grace, a storm that takes 18 condition from the most damaged sanctum (or +4 wood if nothing is damaged), and +2 loyalty to everyone (or +5 grace with no companions).

timer += Time.deltaTime;
if (timer < PhaseSeconds) return;

timer -= PhaseSeconds;
PhaseIndex = (PhaseIndex + 1) % Phases.Length;
if (PhaseIndex == 0) HarvestState.Data.day++;

docs.title: Recruiting companions
docs.text:
A new save starts with companions = 4. Four routes add more, all capped at 30:

  • Build a bed. CreateSanctumAt increments Data.companions, spawns the agent and assigns the bed index to the new record.
  • Rescue a captive. A Rescue room calls RecruitCompanion() when you free the cage. At the cap the room refuses with "The harvest is at its companion cap".
  • Births. Two partners with loyalty ≥ 80 and age ≥ 18 may produce a child at dawn (18% chance, at least three days apart, one birth per dawn).
  • Narrative hooks. RecruitCompanion() is public, so quests and cutscenes can call it directly.

docs.title: The companion record
docs.text:
Every runtime CompanionAgent binds to a serializable CompanionRecord. The agent owns movement and animation; the record owns anything that must survive a save.

Field Type / default Meaning name "" Unique; first eight come from the inner circle trait "Loyal" One of six CompanionTrait values tintR/G/B 0.85, 0.75, 0.95 Sprite tint so generated companions differ hunger 100 0–100, falls 0.30/s loyalty 70 0–100; below 20 the companion is a dissenter exhaustion 0 0–100, rises 0.10/s awake sick false Blocks work bed -1 Index into Data.buildings job -1 Index into Data.buildings priority 0 0 Work, 1 Grace, 2 Social inReflection -1 Index of the reflection chamber holding them mealBuff 0 Seconds of fed bonus remaining (max 180) friend -1 Mutual index pair partner -1 Mutual index pair; prerequisite for children parentA, parentB -1 Biological parents, used for inheritance childDay -1 Day of last child, throttles births age 18–35 Years; incremented at dawn level, xp 1, 0 Levels 1–5, 50 × level xp per level 
public static CompanionRecord CreateCompanionRecord()
{
    var tint = CompanionCatalog.RandomTint();
    return new CompanionRecord
    {
        name = UniqueCompanionName(),
        trait = CompanionCatalog.RandomTrait().ToString(),
        tintR = tint.r, tintG = tint.g, tintB = tint.b,
        hunger = 100f,
        age = UnityEngine.Random.Range(18, 36),
        loyalty = 70f + (Data != null ? Data.metaCharisma * 3 : 0),
        exhaustion = 0f, bed = -1, job = -1
    };
}

EnsureCompanionRecords() is the repair pass. It runs on every load, every recruit and every death: it trims or pads the record list to match Data.companions, fills missing names and traits, clamps every need, repairs records from save schema versions 1 and 2, and renames duplicates.

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
CompanionCatalog.Traits holds six entries. Traits are rolled at random when a record is created and never change afterwards.

Trait Effect in code Loyal loyalty decay multiplied by 0.6 Hardworking WorkBonus starts at 2 instead of 1 Glutton hunger drain × 1.5 Devout GraceBonus +2 at hymns Sickly illness chance 35% per check instead of 8% Lazy exhaustion rises 0.15/s instead of 0.10/s

WorkBonus is the number that feeds building output: (Hardworking ? 2 : 1) + (level - 1) / 2 + (mealBuff > 0 ? 1 : 0).

docs.title: Needs and behaviour states
docs.text:
Companions re-decide every 0.8 s in Decide(). The agent has twelve modes:

Mode Entered when Wander Nothing else applies; picks a random point near home Attend Called by a ceremony; walks to a seat and sets Arrived Work Has a Job; stands at Job.WorkSpot Sleep Night with a bed, or exhaustion ≥ 85 Rest Night without a bed, or RestNow() Eat Hunger < 25 and food or meals exist Haul The assigned workplace has ≥ 4 stored (2 for herb gardens) Clean Idle and a shrine is dirtier than 25 Repair Idle and a sanctum is below 99.5 condition Reflection Confined in a reflection chamber Social Dusk, priority Social, and a tea house exists Pray Dusk, priority Grace, and a shrine exists

The numbers in TickNeeds are the whole survival loop:

  • Hunger falls 0.30/s; sleeping slows it to 30%, reflection to 55%.
  • At hunger 0 a 45-second starvation timer starts; when it expires the companion dies and calls CompanionDied(this).
  • Exhaustion rises 0.10/s awake and falls 3.2/s asleep. Sleeping ends when it drops below 30 or it is no longer night.
  • Loyalty drifts +0.012/s, or -0.065/s while hungry, ill or exhausted past 90.
  • Illness is checked every 12 s when hunger < 25 or exhaustion > 85.
  • Working earns 1 xp/s.

A companion cannot work while sick, dissenting, under 18, or in any mode other than idle/work — that is the CanWork property. Children therefore wander and eat but never staff a building.

docs.title: Feeding, rest and healing
docs.text:
Action Cost Effect Feed() (menu, food) 1 food hunger 100, +6 loyalty, 30 s fed buff EatFood() (automatic) 1 food hunger +55, +1 loyalty EatMeal() (automatic or menu) 1 meal hunger +80, +4 loyalty, 90 s fed buff RestNow() free Rest for 12 s at the bed Treat() 1 medicine cures illness, −20 exhaustion, +5 loyalty Bless() 5 grace −25 exhaustion, +15 loyalty, cures illness

Meals are always eaten before raw food, both in the automatic Eat branch (ConsumeFoodFor) and in the roster's Feed action.

docs.title: Illness and dissent
docs.text:
Sickness is a state, not a timer: it persists until Treat(), Bless(), CeremonyType.Warding, or a natural recovery roll. Recovery needs hunger > 60 and exhaustion < 35, then ticks at roughly 1% per second after 18 seconds ill.

Dissent is simply Loyalty < 20. A dissenter stops working, refuses to socialise, and toasts once ("is losing grace"). Two things fix it: time in a reflection chamber, which adds +0.14 loyalty/s and releases at 45 loyalty or after about 40 seconds, or Bless() / Warding / a funeral.

docs.title: Relationships, children and ageing
docs.text:
TrySocialize() runs every 18 s, or every 12 s when a tea house stands, and pairs two unpartnered companions within 3 m (5 m with a tea house) as friends. TryRomance() runs every 30 s and upgrades a mutual friendship to partners. Both writes are symmetric: A.friend == B and B.friend == A.

TryBirths() requires mutual partners, both aged 18+, both loyalty ≥ 80, three days since either partner's last child, and an 18% roll. The child is appended to the record list with age = 0, loyalty 85, and a tint averaged from both parents. Children age one year per in-game day and become workers at 18.

When a parent dies, the eldest child present inherits the bed and the job if both are free — CompanionDied looks for parentA/parentB matches before creating the memorial.

docs.title: Death and memorials
docs.text:
A MemorialData is appended for every death, with the name, the day, and a position: inside a SanctumType.Memorial aura if one exists, otherwise wherever the companion fell. Surviving companions lose 8 loyalty, and every relationship index pointing at the dead companion is cleared or shifted down.

Interacting with a grave offers:

Choice Cost Effect Mourn free, once +10 grace, +5 loyalty to every survivor Hold a funeral 5 food + 10 grace, once +12 loyalty and −12 exhaustion to everyone Remember free Flavour text; the grave stays named

docs.title: The roster screen
docs.text:
Press F in the hub. ShowCompanionRoster pages five companions at a time and prints one line each:

Amara   •   Lv1 A28   •   Content   •   Rose Garden   •   H100 L70

Choosing a name opens ShowCompanionActions, six entries: Assign job, Feed, Treat, Duty, Bed / Rest, and Reflection. Duty holds the three priorities plus Bless. Bed lists "Rest here now" and the first four beds, with the current sleeper shown; taking an occupied bed evicts the previous owner.

docs.title: The generated companion pool
docs.text: CompanionCatalog ships 30 names. The first eight — Amara, Sable, Iris, Nadia, Yara, Liora, Mira, Yafit — are the inner circle: they are assigned first, and each has portrait art under Resources/Art/Characters/. Amara intentionally reuses the shared companion.png. Every later companion draws from the full pool with a check for duplicates, and falls back to the generic sprite plus the record tint.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
The agent binds the record once, then mirrors every write back through SyncRecord():

public void BindRecord(CompanionRecord record)
{
    Record = record;
    Trait = CompanionCatalog.Parse(record == null ? "Loyal" : record.trait);
    UpdateAppearance();
}

Auto-assignment happens at build time, not by the player: CreateSanctumAt calls TryAssignWorker(built), and AssignWorkers() re-fills every empty workplace after a load or a removal. AssignBeds() does the same for beds. A companion who loses a building through RemoveSanctum is explicitly unassigned, and every stored index is shifted down.

Extending the court

Because CompanionRecord is a plain [Serializable] class, adding a field is a two-step job: add it to the class, then clamp or default it inside EnsureCompanionRecords. The save system does not need to know about it — JsonUtility serialises the whole object graph.
